steps: Inspect & unpack
Inspect the stove for damage and don't install it if any is evident. Confirm the contents, including the dripless pipe adaptor and combustor probe.

Contact the dealer immediately if any damage is found. Do not install a damaged stove.

  • Door Knob Kit (installed on stove)
  • Dripless Pipe Adaptor
  • Smoke Outlet (installed on stove)
  • Hardware Kit
  • Bottom Heat Shield (installed on stove)
  • Combustor Probe

Check permit and inspection requirements with local building or fire officials (NFPA 211 in the U.S., CAN/CSA-B365 in Canada). Do not install in a transportable building (p. 4). Overall dimensions appear only on the drawings, Figs. 1.1–1.3 on this page.
Set the flue exit

Top exit: secure the smoke outlet to the top plate with the pre-installed screws. Rear exit: move the outlet to the back plate using the cover plate's screws and 10mm nuts (reached through the top opening), fit the cover plate on top, then screw the dripless adaptor into the outlet.
Fit accessories before final placement
Install the Rear Heatshield HS-50 (top exit only) and, if used, the Fresh Air Adaptor 156408 (requires the HS-50) before the stove goes into its final position.

The HS-50 can only be used in the top exit mode: the flue collar moves from the rear to the top, and the outlet cover from the top to the rear. Kit: rear heat shield, M6 x 80 bolts (2), M6 nuts (2), washers (2), 2" spacers (2).

  1. Remove the two smoke outlet cover screws and lift the cover off the top.
  2. Through the outlet opening, remove the flue collar nuts and screws (10 mm wrench, screwdriver). Keep the nuts.
  3. Install the flue collar on top with the screws just removed.
  4. Place the outlet cover on the back; insert the two M6 x 80 kit bolts through the back plate from inside the stove and secure with the kit washers and nuts.
  5. Fit the two spacers over the bolts and secure the shield with the nuts kept from step 2.
Step 4 on p. 6 prints M6 x 60 for these bolts; the kit contents and step 5 on the same page give M6 x 80.

The Fresh Air Adaptor valve assembly screws to the back of the heat shield (p. 7); see the outside air spec.
Chimney connector
6" single-wall black steel, 24 gauge minimum, crimped ends toward the stove and three sheet metal screws per joint. Max 36" horizontal rising 1/4" per foot, no more than two 90° elbows.
Qualify the chimney

Use a code-approved masonry chimney and flue liner, or a prefabricated Type HT (2100°F) chimney per UL 103. An existing chimney must pass a UL 1482 Level II inspection; no other appliance on the flue.
Wall pass-through (if needed)
Use an approved method: NFPA 211 in the U.S., CAN/CSA-B365 in Canada. Confirm it with local building officials first.

U.S. common method (NFPA 211)

  • Remove all combustibles at least 12" around the connector location; with a 6" round liner the minimum area is 31" x 31" square.
  • Fill with at least 12" of brick around a fireclay liner (ASTM C35 or equivalent, 5/8" minimum wall). Solid brick, minimum 3 1/4" thick (4" nominal).
  • Locate the pass-through at least 18" from the ceiling. Cut studs, install headers and a sill frame to carry the brick.
  • Refractory mortar at the chimney / pass-through liner junction; the pass-through liner must not extend past the inner surface of the chimney liner.

Canada common method (CAN/CSA-B365, p. 11)

  • Clear combustibles at least 18" around the connector; a 6" round liner needs a minimum 43" x 43" opening.
  • At least 18" from combustible ceiling materials. The cleared space stays empty; sheet metal covers on both sides go on noncombustible spacers at least 1" off the wall (a single panel may be flush).
Connect to the chimney

Masonry thimble: slide the connector fully inside to the inner surface of the flue liner without protruding, and seal with refractory cement. Prefab: use the chimney maker's adaptor and three sheet metal screws.

Masonry thimble

Thimble lined with ceramic tile or metal and securely cemented. The connector slides completely inside to the inner surface of the flue liner but must not protrude into it. A slip-connector may be used. Seal at the thimble with refractory cement; three sheet metal screws at every joint.

Hearth-mount through a masonry fireplace (p. 12)

NFPA 211 (12.4.5.1) requires the flue to be sealed off from room air: replace the damper with a fixed steel plate the connector passes through to the flue tile, or fit a non-combustible plate at the fireplace opening, sealed with high-temperature sealant; or run a full listed liner from the stove to a sealed chimney cap. Rear-exit flue collar height is 21 5/8" with standard legs. Reline a flue that is too large, and keep the tested trim / mantel clearances and floor protection.

Do not install in any fireplace. The stove may vent through a masonry fireplace but must sit in front of the opening, and must not be installed in a factory-built fireplace.

Prefabricated chimney (p. 12)

Follow the chimney maker's instructions and use all required components. The adaptor on the bottom chimney section takes the connector with three sheet metal screws.
Floor protection

Leave the supplied bottom heat shield installed and lay Type I continuous non-combustible protection, minimum 28 1/2"W X 43 1/2"D (U.S.) or 28 1/2"W X 45 1/2"D (Canada); for a rear vent, extend it 2" beyond either side of the pipe.
Set clearances
Place the stove using the clearance chart for your pipe type and heat-shield setup; alcoves need listed double-wall pipe. Never block airflow in the clearance space.

The chart values are UL/ULC-tested minimums from the stove to any combustible surface, including materials behind non-combustible facings. "Fire resistant" materials and fire-rated sheet rock count as combustible.

  • Choose the row for single wall, shielded single wall or double wall pipe, with or without the Rear Heatshield HS-50.
  • Alcoves: top exit, listed double-wall pipe, and the minimum alcove dimensions.
  • Only listed clearance-reduction accessories carrying a testing laboratory's mark; for this stove's rear, only the HS-50.
  • Mantel and trim clearances are shown only as a diagram (Fig. 4.14, p. 18).
Fit the combustor monitor

Remove the set screw on the right side panel with a 3mm hex key, turn the monitor's magnet to the correct orientation, and push the monitor fully into the hole so the magnet holds to the cast iron side plate.

1. Remove the set screw on the right side panel of the stove with a 3mm hex key.
  2. Take the magnet off the Combustor Monitor and refit it in the correct orientation; the orientation is shown only in Figs. 5.6–5.8 (p. 22).
  3. Insert the monitor fully into the hole, with the magnet attaching to the cast iron side plate.

Seated in the right side directly behind the catalytic element, it reads combustion activity. Replacement: Combustor Monitor PN 226609.

panels.title: Weak draft · smoke in the room
items: Weak or erratic draft → back puffing: smoke leaks out through stove or connector joints
Chimney shorter than 14 feet → smoke spills when loading or with the door open
Short exterior masonry chimney → hard to hold draft; reline or extend it in very cold areas
Exhaust fan or clothes dryer → low room pressure, flow reversal through stove and chimney

panels.title: Strong draft · over-firing
items: Excessive draft → high stove temperatures, short burn times; a butterfly damper corrects it
Any part of the stove or connector glowing (not the combustor) → over-firing
Door left partly open → over-firing; flame and smoke drawn out
After the fact: warped plates, rust-colored cast iron, dusty-white paint, cracked enamel

panels.title: Combustor not performing
items: Monitor won't stay at 500°F after 2–3 hours at medium to high, air at medium to medium low → clean or replace
Junk mail or copious newsprint as starter → faster fly-ash buildup on the combustor
Non-functioning combustor → lower efficiency, more creosote and emissions

panels.title: Smoky, smoldering fire
items: Wood over 20% moisture → heat lost to evaporation, creosote, weak draft
Weak kindling fire → larger pieces don't catch; inefficient, smoldering fire
Smoldering, smoky fire → higher CO; keep a well-established fire
Wood seasoned more than 2 years → burns too quickly

start.title: Starting a fire (top-down)
start.html:
Build every fire right on the floor of the firebox. Don't use a grate or raise the fire, and don't build it close to the door glass.

The top-down method makes less start-up smoke and gets a strong draft going quickly:

  1. Slide the primary air lever fully to the right (full open).
  2. Lay two short 1/4-split logs on the firebox floor about 6 inches apart, running front to back.
  3. Lay kindling across those two logs.
  4. Set one or two smaller logs on top of the kindling.
  5. Tuck newspaper between the two bottom logs, under the kindling. Light it and close the door.
  6. Add kindling and small logs as needed. Keep the air fully open until the fire is well established.
Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or "freshen up" a fire. Keep them away from the stove at all times.
Brand-new stove? Do the three break-in fires first.

breakin.title: First fires: the break-in
breakin.html:
Your stove is built from cast iron plates sealed with furnace cement. Cast iron expands and contracts as it heats and cools, so a new stove is broken in with a short series of small-to-medium fires. Watch a stove-top thermometer as you go.

  1. Open the primary air fully. Light a small fire of newspaper and kindling. Let the stove top reach only 200°F, hold it there for about 1 hour, then let the stove cool to room temperature.
  2. Light a second fire and let the stove reach no more than 400°F for 1 hour.
  3. Let it cool to room temperature.
  4. Light a third fire and gradually bring the stove up to 500°F, and hold it there.
  5. Let it cool to room temperature. Break-in is done.
Getting too hot? Keep every break-in fire except the last under 400°F. If it goes over, slide the air lever all the way left. The temperature may keep climbing until the wood burns down a bit; that's normal. Never pull burning logs out to cool it down.

Smell and smoke at first

A new painted stove can give off an odor and some smoke during the first fires as the high-temperature paint cures. Open a window or door for extra air.

air.title: Setting the air control
air.html:
The primary air lever slides in the door, just under the glass. It sets how much air feeds the fire, so it controls how hot it burns and how long a load lasts. Secondary air is automatic: a heat-sensitive coil at the back of the stove adjusts it for you.

LeftClosed · low burn, minimum fire
MiddleMedium burn
RightFull open · high burn, maximum fire
  • Starting or reviving a fire: fully right. For a low or medium burn, still leave it fully right for the first five minutes.
  • With the combustor monitor: stay fully right until it reads 500°F, hold that for 15–20 minutes, then set it between medium-low and medium-high. The best range for clean burning is 500°F to 800°F.
  • With a stove-top thermometer in either rear corner, 400°F–600°F is the best range; once there, a middle setting keeps the fire efficient. 700–800°F for short spells won't harm the stove, but long spells can.
Note: p. 22 gives the upper end of the optimum monitor range as 800° and pairs it with 371°C; those two figures don't match.
Keep the door fully closed while it burns. A door left partly open can over-fire the stove and draw flame and smoke into the room.

reload.title: Reloading & clearing ashes
reload.html:
Reload while there's still a bed of hot embers.

  1. Put on gloves and push the air lever fully right (full open).
  2. Open the door slightly first, then fully. This lets the airflow settle so less smoke spills out.
  3. Spread the hot embers evenly with a poker or stove tool.
  4. Load the wood, usually smaller logs first. Don't load higher than the holes in the air baffle; the traditional three-log load is safest and looks best.
  5. Close the door and latch it tightly.
  6. Wait 5–10 minutes, then set the air for the heat you want. With an ember bed at least 2" thick, you may be able to set it right away.

Ashes

Expect to clear ashes every day or two. It's easiest once the fire has burned down to coals. Wearing stove gloves, use a long-handled shovel: push the coals to one side, shovel out the ash, then repeat on the other side. Spread the remaining coals across the floor to light the next fire quickly.

Keep ashes in a metal container with a tight lid, used only for ashes. Leave it closed, outdoors and away from anything that burns, until every cinder is completely cool.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn natural, untreated wood only. Air-dried, seasoned hardwood gives the cleanest, most efficient heat. Logs can be up to 16" long.

  • Seasoning: wood air-dried for 6 to 14 months is best. Wood seasoned more than 2 years burns too quickly to make the most of the stove at low burn.
  • How to tell: a seasoned log has many cracks (check marks) through the ends and feels lighter. A moisture meter with probes should read 12–20%.
  • Why it matters: wet wood spends its heat boiling off water, and that moisture condenses as creosote in the chimney, raising the risk of a chimney fire.
  • Store wood somewhere dry, outside the stove's clearance area.

Never burn

Coal, garbage, synthetic logs, anything with rubber or plastic, waste petroleum products, asphalt products, paints, paint thinners or solvents, asbestos, construction debris, railroad ties or pressure-treated wood, manure or animal remains, yard waste, salt-water driftwood, unseasoned wood, colored paper, junk mail, cardboard, plywood or particle board. Paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax fire starters are fine for lighting.

These can give off toxic fumes, including carbon monoxide, damage the catalytic combustor and void your warranty.
The manual prints 508 mm beside the 16" log length on p. 3; the two don't match, and the maker's website gives Log size 16 in.

combustor.title: Caring for the catalytic combustor
combustor.html:
The catalytic combustor sits above the baffle at the top of the firebox and burns off gases that would otherwise go up the chimney unburned. It's durable but needs regular checks. Federal rules prohibit running the stove with it removed or deactivated.

Signs it's working

  • Above 500°F, look up through the glass: jets of flame come from the baffle ports and the catalyst glows bright red.
  • Little or no smoke leaves the chimney, and sweeping brings down mostly fly ash.

Routine care

  • Look at it at least three times each heating season: open the door and look up with a flashlight.
  • Brush fly ash off the cells with a soft brush. A shop vacuum can be used carefully; the cells are fragile.
  • Junk mail or lots of newspaper as a fire starter clogs it faster.

Heat seems weak?

Burn at medium to high for two or three hours, over 500°F, to build a full bed of coals. Set the air to medium or medium-low. If the monitor won't stay at 500°F or higher, the combustor may need cleaning or replacing. Repeat the test 2–3 times to be sure. Parts come from your authorized Jøtul dealer; the replacement catalytic combustor is part 158375.

The accessories list on p. 2 prints the replacement catalyst as 158735; the parts list on p. 29 gives 158375.

glass.title: Glass & door seal
glass.html:
The air wash and normal high temperatures keep the glass mostly clear, but now and then you'll need to clean off carbon and fly ash. Left too long, those deposits can etch the glass and make it cloudy.

  • Use only an ammonia-free, non-abrasive stove glass cleaner.
  • Never clean hot glass. Clean it only at room temperature.
  • The glass is fragile. Don't strike it or slam the door.
  • Keep logs from resting directly on the glass.
Broken glass? Don't run the stove. Replace it only with genuine Jøtul ceramic glass (128101), never a substitute.

Check the door seal

Close and latch the door on a dollar bill, then slowly pull it out. If it comes out easily, the seal is too loose. Try several spots around the door. The Universal Gasket Kit (157050) from your dealer has what's needed to replace the gaskets.

chimney.title: Creosote & chimney fires
chimney.html:
Slow fires and green wood produce tar and vapors that condense in the chimney as creosote. Creosote is highly flammable; it's the fuel of chimney fires.

Keep it swept

  • Inspect the chimney and connector at the start of each heating season, then every other month while you're burning.
  • Clean whenever creosote and fly ash build up past 1/4 inch anywhere in the system.
  • Hotter fires leave less creosote. You may need weekly cleaning in mild weather; monthly may be enough in the coldest months.
  • Your dealer can refer you to a professional chimney sweep.

If the chimney catches fire

You may hear a roaring noise and crackling as burning creosote breaks loose.

  1. Slide the air lever fully left (closed) right away and make sure the door is shut.
  2. Call the fire department and get everyone safely out of the house.
  3. Don't try to put out the fire in the stove; that feeds the chimney fire more air.
  4. When the noise dies down, don't open the door to check. The fire could flare up again.
Don't use the stove again until the chimney and connector have been cleaned and inspected for damage.

safety.title: Safety & over-firing
safety.html:
• The stove is extremely hot while it runs. Keep children, clothing and furniture away, and use a child guard screen for small children.
  • Put smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) detectors in the living area and bedrooms. Test them regularly and change the batteries twice a year. Jøtul also highly recommends a CO detector in the stove's room, placed as far from the stove as possible so it doesn't go off when you open the door to add wood.
  • Run the stove only with the door fully closed.
  • Exhaust fans and clothes dryers can pull air backward through the stove and chimney. Talk to your dealer if this happens.
  • The low burn rate is set at the factory. Altering it is against federal regulations.

Signs you're over-firing

Do not over-fire the stove. If any part of the stove or chimney connector glows, except the combustor, you're over-firing. That can cause a house fire or serious damage, and it can void your warranty. Afterward, over-firing shows up as warped plates, rust-colored cast iron, paint that has turned dusty white, or bubbling, cracking or discolored enamel.

The combustor's maximum recommended temperature is 1600°F (870°C). Going over 1750°F (954°C), even briefly, can damage it.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Jøtul North America warrants these parts to the original retail purchaser, from the date of purchase:

Baffle & air manifoldLifetime, parts only
Cast iron & steel parts5 years
Enamel finish (peeling, fading)2 years
Electrical, incl. combustion monitor1 year
Catalytic combustor10 years, separate warranty

For the combustor, the first replacement for a defect is free, a second failure within 10 years is 50% off current retail, and later ones are at current retail. Installation, travel and shipping are yours to pay.

Not covered

  • Normal wear parts: paint, gaskets, burn plates, baffles, air manifolds, glass (covered only against thermal breakage)
  • Installation or service not done by an authorized installer, or not per the manual and codes
  • Over-firing, misuse, unauthorized changes, damage in transit
To claim, contact your authorized Jøtul dealer. Jøtul must get notice within 60 days of finding a defect. Keep your dated receipt.
Note: p. 30 says Jøtul will repair or replace covered parts "including parts & labor", while p. 31 limits its liability to the cost of a replacement part and excludes labor by others.

specOutput.title: Heat output & fuel
specOutput.html:
Heat output range5,994 to 23,415 BTU/hr. (2.0-7.3 kW)
Maker's website: Max Output (kW): 37.5.
Heating capacityUp to 800 sq. ft.
Maximum burn timeUp to 5 hours
FuelSolid wood only · up to 16" logs
CombustionCatalytic combustor, automatic secondary air

Output range comes from EPA emissions testing; heating capacity and burn time vary with the home, chimney, climate, wood type and operation. Build the fire directly on the firebox floor; no grate.

The manual prints Up to 16" Logs (508 mm) on p. 3; 508 mm doesn't match 16". The maker's website gives Log size 16 in.

specEff.title: Efficiency & emissions
specEff.html:

EPA efficiency, LHV82.9%

Meets the 2020 U.S. EPA emission limits for wood heaters. Efficiencies per CSA B415.1-10. Listed to ANSI/UL 1482 (U.S.) and CAN/ULC-S627 and CAN/ULC 628 (Canada); safety tests by Intertek, Middleton, WI; EPA tests by PFS-TECO, Portland, OR.

Section 5.1 on p. 18 gives the same EPA HHV efficiency without the decimal, as 76%; the combustion specifications on p. 3 give 76.7%.

specConnector.title: Chimney connector
specConnector.html:
Diameter6"
MaterialSingle-wall black steel, 24 gauge minimum
Max horizontal run36"
Recommended total lengthNot over 10 feet
SlopeUp 1/4" per foot toward the chimney
ElbowsNo more than two 90°
Rear-exit collar height21 5/8" with standard legs (p. 12)

Crimped (male) ends toward the stove; three sheet metal screws at every joint; flue collar to connector with 2 self-drilling screws from the kit. No aluminum or galvanized pipe. Keep every section accessible for cleaning, and never run it through an attic, roof space, closet or other concealed space, or through a floor or ceiling. Don't use the connector as a chimney or join a flue serving another appliance.

specChimney.title: Chimney
specChimney.html:
Minimum height15 feet
Above roof penetrationAt least 3 feet
Above roof or structure within 10 feetAt least 2 feet
PrefabHT, UL 103 (U.S.) · ULC S629 (Canada)
Flue areaNot less than the flue collar; not more than three times (two times with an exterior wall below the roofline)
Fireclay liner8" X 8" nominal, not larger than 8" X 12"; round 6" to 8" inside; 5/8" min. thickness
Draft.05 - 1.0 w.c. (as printed, p. 22)

An existing chimney must pass a UL 1482 Level II inspection by a qualified technician or building official (p. 8). Masonry: refractory mortar, 1/4" air space between liner and chimney wall, brick or block walls 4" nominal or stone 12", an airtight clean-out door at the base, and no other appliance on the flue (p. 9). Prefab clearance to combustibles per the pipe maker, usually a minimum of 2". Excessive draft can be corrected with a butterfly damper.

Note: p. 10 gives a minimum chimney height of 15 feet, and the next paragraph says chimneys shorter than 14 feet may not provide adequate draft.
Note: p. 8 gives a Canada-only liner rule, This fireplace insert must be installed with a continuous chimney liner of 6" diameter (CAN/ULC-S635 Class 3 or CAN/ULC-S640), while p. 12 says the F 602 V3 must not be installed in any fireplace.

specAlcove.html:

Vertical venting, top exit assumed. Listed double-wall pipe is required. In a protected alcove both side walls and the rear wall are protected per NFPA 211; the protection sits 1" off the floor and at least 1" off the combustible wall, and is 48" tall including the bottom air space. Ceiling (p. 15): minimum ceiling height in an unprotected installation is 60" from the floor; with a protected ceiling, the minimum is 15" off the top of the stove. The alcove drawings with lettered dimensions are on p. 15.

conflicts.reason: Same EPA HHV efficiency: section 5.1 (p. 18) states it without the decimal as 76%; the combustion specifications (p. 3) give 76.7%. Both shown, worded as one figure.

conflicts.issue: Minimum chimney height 15 feet vs 'Chimneys shorter than 14 feet may not provide adequate draft' in the next paragraph.

'Canada Only: This fireplace insert must be installed with a continuous chimney liner of 6" diameter…' (appears to be carried over from an insert manual) vs 'DO NOT INSTALL IN ANY FIREPLACE' / stove must sit in front of the opening.
Floor protector extensions: text gives U.S. 16" front / 8" sides and Canada 18" front / 8" side and back, but captions read Fig. 4.1 'A is 6" B is 16"' and Fig. 4.2 'A is 8" B is 16"'.
Fresh air adaptor 'includes a 3 inch adapter' (accessories) vs 4" dia. conduit, 4" hose clamp and 4" hole saw (installation section).
Outside air kit number: Fresh Air Adaptor 156408 vs 'optional Outside Air Kit #154335' in the safety notices.
HS-50 bolts: kit contents and step 5 list M6 x 80; step 4 says M6 x 60.
Replacement catalyst part number: 158735 (Accessories) vs 158375 (parts list item 57, Catalyst Combustor).
Optimum combustor monitor range printed as '500°F and 800° (260°C -371°C)'; the °F and °C upper limits don't match.
Jøtul 'will repair or replace (including parts & labor)' vs liability 'limited exclusively to the cost of furnishing a replacement component' and no liability for labor by others.

review.notes: Single 36-page manual (pp. 33-35 blank). Page refs are physical pages; printed footers match, but the table of contents and several cross-references point 2 pages low or to the wrong section (e.g. 'Section 2.3 on page 7' is p. 9; clearance 'pages 14-15' are pp. 15-17; 'Break-in Procedure, Sect. 5.6' is 5.7; 'figure 4.15 pg 17' is on p. 18). Catalog check: output 5,994-23,415 BTU/hr, 800 sq ft, 76.7% HHV, 1.4 g/hr, EPA 2020, catalytic, 5 hr burn, 16" logs, 6" flue, outside air available and not for transportable buildings all match. Not stated in the manual: weight (catalog 160 lb unverified), firebox volume, and labeled overall dimensions - the p. 5 drawings show only unlabeled callouts (25 1/4", 21 1/4", 12 5/8", 21 5/8", etc.), consistent with catalog H/D/W but not confirmable, so no dimension card. Mantel/trim clearance (Fig. 4.14, p. 18) and the HS-50 magnet orientation (Figs. 5.6-5.8) are diagrams only; linked, not transcribed. Lettered alcove/clearance figures on pp. 15 and 17 were not transcribed beyond values matching the p. 16 table; Fig. 4.6 'B: Max. 24"' (alcove with rear heat shield) and Fig. 4.9/4.12 values (19", 20 1/4", 24") are unexplained in the text, and Fig. 4.3 pairs 60" with 244 cm. Alcove ceiling: p. 15 gives 60" from the floor (unprotected) and 15" off the stove top (protected ceiling); the p. 16 table gives 35" above the stove for unprotected and protected surfaces - shown with their own conditions, not flagged. The clearance chart covers top vent / vertical only; no rear-exit clearances are given in text. Chimney draft '.05 - 1.0 w.c.' (p. 22) reproduced as printed; looks like a possible typo, confirm with Jotul. Standards typos: 'CASN/ULC-S627' (p. 3) shown as CAN/ULC-S627; p. 11 cites both CAN/CSA-B365 and 'CSA-B635'. 'UL 1482 Level II inspection' (p. 8) reproduced as printed. mm equivalents vary (6" = 152 mm on p. 8, 157 mm on pp. 9-10); the guide uses the manual's inch figures. Section 6.4 Enamel Care is in the TOC but has no text; combustor replacement steps skip step 2 (p. 27). The manual mentions an ash pan / ash pan door (pp. 24-25) but ash removal uses a shovel and the parts list has no ash pan; not used. Warranty lists baffles and air manifolds both under the lifetime defect warranty and among wear parts excluded; shown as written. No blower is described (warranty mentions blowers generically). No troubleshooting chart or code table: fault panels are built from the manual's draft, over-firing, fuel and combustor-test descriptions; codes empty. No French-only or scrambled text.
